newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says gun deaths down, traffic deaths up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says gun deaths down, traffic deaths up.

text.p: Road deaths in the United States have begun to increase while gun deaths have declined markedly, reversing long-standing trends in both cases, federal health officials said on Thursday.

In a report profiling the nation's health, the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said traffic accidents, firearms and poisonings were the leading causes of deaths from injuries in 1995.
The CDC's National Centre for Health Statistics said age- adjusted firearm mortality, which increased 22 percent between 1985 and 1993, declined 11 percent between 1993 and 1995.
Motor vehicle fatality rates, which declined 15 percent between 1985 and 1993, rose two percent between 1993 and 1995. Preliminary data indicated the two trends continued through June 1996.

The CDC said that 6 percent of all deaths in 1995 were injury-related. "Injuries cause more deaths among youth than disease or natural causes," Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said in a statement.
The CDC report also said life expectancy at birth had continued to increase for Americans, reaching 75.8 years, up from 75.7 years in 1994.
The homicide rate for black Americans in 1996 was six times the rate for whites and the AIDS death rate was almost five times that of whites, the CDC said.

The health agency said enrollment in health maintenance organisations rose 14 percent to 52.5 million people, an increase of 6.3 million over 1995. It said most of the increase was because Medicaid enrollees were making greater use of them.
